one_liner: Dependency-free YuNet CNN face detector; its 2026 Highway build is 2.8-3.9x faster single-thread than the project's own AVX2 original.
what_it_does: libfacedetection detects faces (box, score and five landmarks) in a BGR image with the YuNet CNN, whose weights are compiled into src/facedetectcnn-data.cpp, and writes them into a caller-supplied 0x9000-byte result buffer via facedetect_cnn(buffer, bgr, width, height, step). The highway/ subproject (May 2026) adds facedetect_hw_cnn with the same arguments and the same 16-short-per-face result layout (capped at 1024 faces), built as a separate CMake library on Google Highway 1.3.0. A pure-Rust reimplementation, libfacedetection_rs, lives in rust/ with a safe Detector::detect API over the image crate.
how_it_is_fast: The original computes each 1x1 (pointwise) output channel as a separate dot product with a horizontal reduction (_mm256_mul_ps/_mm256_add_ps plus hadd, no FMA) and allocates fresh blobs for every layer on every call. The Highway path repacks pointwise weights into output-channel blocks at model load and runs a register-blocked outer-product kernel (broadcast one input value, FMA into 2-8 vector accumulators, 64-output specialisation); on x86 the 'hybrid' build swaps in AVX2/FMA intrinsics for 3x3 depthwise and max-pool with fused ReLU and an interior fast path. It also fuses FPN upsample+add and keeps the model in a function-local static and all activations in thread_local workspaces, removing per-call allocation and zeroing; highway/docs/hw-performance-report.md credits the packed pointwise kernel and workspace reuse with the largest gains.
when_to_use: CPU-only face detection on x86-64 where you build per instruction set (AVX2 hybrid is the fastest measured build: 8.48 ms at 640x480, 0.32 ms at 128x96 single-thread on an i7-14700KF).
Small-input real-time pipelines (320x240 or smaller) that need sub-millisecond to ~2 ms detection without a general inference engine.
Many concurrent camera streams handled by calling facedetect_hw_cnn from several threads, one result buffer per thread.
Existing facedetect_cnn users who want a near drop-in speedup: same arguments, same result-buffer layout, same post-processing thresholds (0.45/0.2, top-k 1000/512).
Rust projects that want a self-contained detector with runtime AVX2 dispatch and a scalar fallback (as a git dependency; see gotchas).
when_not_to_use: ARM or Apple Silicon: the Highway version has not been tested on ARM, the published ARM numbers are for the original on a Raspberry Pi 4, and issue #376 reports the original's NEON path being ineffective on ARMv8-A.
One binary for mixed x86 fleets: Highway static targets with no runtime dispatch, so an AVX2 build requires AVX2+FMA CPUs; AVX-512 builds compile but were never measured.

Choosing between detectors or runtimes: there is no comparison against OpenCV FaceDetectorYN (same YuNet model), ncnn, MNN, OpenVINO, dlib or RetinaFace, so the gain over running YuNet in an existing engine is unknown.
Accuracy-critical or tiny-face workloads: YuNet scores AP_easy 0.887, AP_medium 0.871, AP_hard 0.768 on WIDER Face (README), with a minimum face size of about 10x10.
GCC or Clang builds from before 2026-06-28: AVX2+ targets segfaulted in five Highway kernels that used aligned loads on 16-byte-aligned std::vector data (fixed by PR #383).

integration.dependencies: original: none (copy src/ into the project); Highway version: Google Highway 1.3.0 via find_package(hwy 1.3.0), OpenCV only for the benchmarks and examples; Rust crate: image 0.25.10 (jpeg, png)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (cxx_std_11) and CMake 3.15 for highway/; README numbers from MSVC 19.40 (VS 2022); Rust 1.85, edition 2024, for the crate
integration.platforms: x86-64 measured (Windows, MSVC; scalar, SSE/default and AVX2 builds); AVX-512 buildable but unmeasured; ARM untested for the Highway version
integration.thread_safety: facedetect_hw_cnn is safe to call concurrently (function-local static model, thread_local workspaces) as long as each thread has its own result buffer; each thread's workspaces stay allocated for the thread's lifetime. The original facedetect_cnn initialises its global filters through an unsynchronised param_initialized flag, so make one call before going multi-threaded.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same arguments and result layout as facedetect_cnn, but a different header (facedetect_hw.h) and function name, a separate CMake project and a Highway 1.3.0 dependency

gotchas: Harness flaw in the C++ multi-thread rows: hw_resolution_benchmark.cpp starts the timer before creating the 28 std::threads, runs only 128 iterations in total (4-5 per thread), and its warm-up calls run on the main thread, so each new thread's first facedetect_hw_cnn call allocates its thread_local workspaces inside the timed region. The Rust harness warms each worker and starts timing after a barrier, so the README's Rust-versus-C++ multi-thread rows (e.g. 14812.76 vs 6879.46 FPS at 128x96) are not like-for-like; only the single-thread rows are clean comparisons.

The '6.4x speed up' commit title and the 6.9x figure in highway/docs/hw-performance-report.md (269.72 ms vs 38.85 ms at 1280x960) compare against the original built without _ENABLE_AVX2: in highway/CMakeLists.txt only fdt_hw_resolution_benchmark gets the AVX2 definition, not fdt_hw_image_benchmark, and 269.72 ms matches four times the README's scalar 640x480 time (derived from page data). Against the AVX2 original the single-thread gain is 2.8-3.9x.

README numbers (May 2026, MSVC) predate the PR #383 crash fix (aligned to unaligned load/store in MulAddLoop, DotProductHw, AddHw, AddInplaceHw, ReluHw) and were not re-measured; no performance effect is stated.

The README tells Rust users to add libfacedetection_rs = "0.1", but crates.io returns 'crate libfacedetection_rs does not exist' (checked 2026-10-11) and rust/Cargo.toml points its repository at the Wwupup fork, so it must be used as a git or path dependency; it also exposes no C ABI.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over general CPU inference engines such as MNN, OpenVINO, NNPACK or FeatherCNN when the job is only face detection and you want a single self-contained C API with the model baked in; pick those engines when you need other models, ARM-tuned kernels or GPU back ends, since none of them is benchmarked against this detector.
verified_claims_summary: First-party, same-binary benchmark (MSVC 19.40 Release, Highway 1.3.0, Intel Core i7-14700KF, cnnresult.png resized with OpenCV, 128 iterations after 5 warm-ups): the Highway AVX2 hybrid build takes 8.48/2.14/0.53/0.32 ms versus 33.42/7.70/1.49/0.88 ms for the original AVX2 build at 640x480/320x240/160x120/128x96 (about 3.9x to 2.8x), and 7.7x versus the original's non-SIMD build at 640x480. The 28-thread rows (1.9x at 640x480) include thread-creation overhead, and the Rust crate's 4.1x comes from a separate Rust harness.
status_note: Active (BSD-3-Clause, about 12.8k stars). The Highway and Rust paths were added in May 2026 by maintainer Wwupup and last changed by the June 2026 SIGSEGV fix; they are young, x86-only in practice, and the Rust crate is not yet on crates.io.
